note.business: Demand is not the problem. Trailing sales grew 27.53% to 241.6B, and gross margin is 81.03%. However, quarterly growth has slowed from 33.08% two quarters ago to 26.07%. The real issue is cost. Operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) fell from 43.23% to 32.86%. Free cash flow (cash left after spending on the business) fell from 44.8B to 28.6B, so only 11.86% of sales now turns into free cash. The filings also flag that profit per share is trailing sales and that the company missed forecasts by 29% last quarter. The balance sheet is not at risk: liquidity is 82.4B and net cash is close to zero at -1.2B, even with 83.7B of debt. Today's news only affects sentiment. A scheduling feature and a rival's video update do not change demand, margins or cash. The $14.1M of insider sales outside pre-set plans is a governance signal, not a business change. What is at risk is cash generation and margins. Revenue and financial stability are not.

worth.text: The methods disagree because they rest on different assumptions. A discounted-cash-flow model (DCF) values the business on its future cash, starting from today's 28.6B and using a 9.9% discount rate. It gives 244.22 (bear), 379.4 (base) and 517.42 (bull). All three are below 609.89. To justify today's price, free cash flow would have to start growing at about 36.7% a year. Even 30% growth gives only 476.95. Meta's own price-to-sales history gives a much higher range of 475.85–707.21–881.21, because it assumes the market will pay what it usually has relative to sales. On simple multiples the stock is not expensive. It trades at 20.9 times trailing earnings and 6.5 times sales, close to the peer median of 6.1 and at the 30th percentile of its own 5-year range. Cash flow is what separates the two approaches. If margins kept shrinking, the value would fall further: 244.63 at a 24% operating margin. My fair-value range is 475.85–707.21. The current price sits inside it, but only if cash flow recovers.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers toward the earlier 44.8B as the heavy spending pays off, instead of staying near 28.6B.
